analysis.one_liner: Builds and preserves millions of affordable homes and helps first-time buyers in formerly segregated areas, paid for by raising the estate tax on very large inheritances.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2018 and referred to five House committees, where it died without a hearing or vote as the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have spent roughly $50 billion a year on affordable housing: grants to local governments that loosen zoning so more homes can be built, a large fund to construct rental units affordable to middle- and low-income families, down-payment grants for first-time buyers in neighborhoods that were once legally segregated, aid to homeowners still underwater from the 2008 crash, and stronger anti-discrimination and bank-lending rules. To pay for it, the bill rolls back the 2017 estate-tax cut, lowering the exemption to $3.5 million and raising rates to 65% on the largest estates, and closes trust loopholes used to pass wealth to heirs tax-free. It was referred to five committees and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and first-time homebuyers get more affordable options and, in historically redlined areas, federal down-payment grants. Homeowners still underwater from the 2008 crisis get help reducing what they owe. Low-income borrowers and communities gain from stronger fair-housing and bank-lending rules. Construction workers gain from prevailing-wage requirements on funded projects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters, first-time buyers, and struggling homeowners

how_it_helps.text: Spends roughly $50 billion a year building and preserving homes: $44.5 billion a year to the Housing Trust Fund, $2.5 billion a year to the Capital Magnet Fund, $4 billion for a Middle Class Housing Emergency Fund, plus rural and tribal housing funds.
Gives first-time homebuyers in formerly redlined and legally segregated neighborhoods a federal grant of up to 3.5% of the home's value toward a down payment.
Sends $2 billion to states to help homeowners who owe more than their houses are worth after the financial crisis, through loan modifications and principal reduction.

Awards grants to cities and states that rewrite zoning to allow more affordable housing—by-right development, smaller lots, accessory apartments—and requires prevailing (Davis-Bacon) wages on funded construction.

Expands Fair Housing Act protections to cover sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, source of income, and perceived race, and strengthens the Community Reinvestment Act so banks and nonbank mortgage lenders must document how they serve low- and moderate-income communities.

analysis.who_pays: Very wealthy families pay: the bill lowers the estate-tax exemption to $3.5 million, raises rates to 65% on estates above $93 million, adds a 10% surtax on billion-dollar estates, and closes common trust loopholes used to pass wealth to heirs tax-free. Banks and nonbank mortgage lenders also face stronger fair-lending scrutiny.
analysis.who_pays_short: Very large estates and wealthy inheritors

drawbacks.text: The bill is funded through large new appropriations—$44.5 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund, $2 billion a year for zoning-reform grants, and a $4 billion down-payment fund—paid for by raising the estate tax, which Republicans had just cut in 2017 and were certain to resist.

Federal construction subsidies can raise costs where local zoning still blocks new building; the bill tries to counter this with incentives for localities to allow denser housing, but participation is voluntary, so the grants could partially inflate prices instead of lowering them.

The down-payment grants subsidize demand for homes, and some economists would argue direct demand subsidies push sale prices up, particularly in tight markets, unless paired with the kind of supply expansion the bill only encourages rather than requires.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—more affordable homes, help for first-time buyers and underwater borrowers, stronger fair-housing and anti-discrimination protections—are broad and substantial, and the mechanism for paying for them (restoring the estate tax to pre-2017 levels and closing trust loopholes) falls entirely on multi-million-dollar estates. The main drawbacks are real: the bill relies on roughly $50 billion a year in new appropriations, and boosting demand through construction subsidies and down-payment grants without enough new supply can push prices up, which is why the zoning-reform grants matter so much to whether the bill works. But on balance the costs land on those best able to bear them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees in December 2018, none of which ever acted on it, so it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Cedric Richmond on December 11, 2018, in the final weeks of the 115th Congress.

The same day it was referred to five committees—Financial Services, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Education and the Workforce—and on December 13 two subcommittees of Transportation and Infrastructure received referrals.
No committee ever held a hearing, marked up the bill, or reported it out, and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill would have been paid for chiefly by lowering the estate tax exemption to $3.5 million and restoring tax rates of up to 65% on estates above $93 million—provisions opposed by the wealthy households they target and their allies in Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax was not restored, so very wealthy estates and the banks' lighter-touch regulatory treatment continued unchanged; renters and first-time buyers in expensive markets got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy estates and the banking status quo

for.name: Reps. Elijah Cummings, Barbara Lee, and Gwen Moore
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it to the House.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never acted on its estate-tax provisions.

against.name: House Judiciary, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never acted on the provisions in their jurisdictions.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: The bill, backed by Senator Elizabeth Warren's Senate companion, had no path in a Republican-held Senate and was never expected to advance.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill surfaced in the final weeks of a Republican-controlled Congress and died without any vote, so no roll-call ever tested it.

industries.note: Lowers the estate tax exemption to $3.5 million, restores 55-65% rates above that, adds a 10% surtax on billion-dollar estates, and closes GRAT and grantor-trust loopholes used to pass wealth to heirs tax-free.

The bill expands Community Reinvestment Act obligations to cover nonbank lenders, adds data-collection and disclosure duties, and lets regulators downgrade lenders that violate consumer laws—but the same bill also funds housing construction that benefits lenders' mortgage volume.
Billions in federal construction subsidies flow to builders of affordable rental units, with prevailing-wage requirements that also favor organized labor.

Fair Housing Act changes bar landlords from rejecting tenants over source of income (including housing vouchers) and add discrimination categories, but the bill's housing construction also expands the rental market.
